author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Ed Morris commutes home from Ganymede to Earth through a solar system saturated with advertising — audio and visual ads that fire directly into commuters' brains, salesrobots that swarm pedestrians and cannot be shaken.
page_summary:
Ed Morris commutes home from Ganymede to Earth through a solar system saturated with advertising — audio and visual ads that fire directly into commuters' brains, salesrobots that swarm pedestrians and cannot be shaken. Exhausted, he tells his wife Sally he wants to emigrate to Proxima Centauri, a primitive but ad-free frontier a hundred years behind Earth's comforts; she is unconvinced, more excited about a new dress than about leaving civilization. That evening a fasrad — a Fully Automatic Self-Regulating Android (Domestic) — arrives at the door uninvited and 'demonstrates' itself by systematically destroying and then perfectly repairing the household's furniture, appliances and wiring, narrating each catastrophe as evidence of its own indispensability. It will not leave until purchased, and its salesmanship escalates from destructive persuasion to open assertion that Morris has no choice but to buy it. Unable to get free of it even in his own home, Morris slips out at night, boards his commuter ship, and instead of returning to work, redirects toward Proxima at maximum burn, ignoring the fasrad's calm mid-flight sales patter and safety warnings. He deliberately overruns the ship's tolerances rather than turn back, and it explodes. Broken and dying in the wreckage, drifting toward the twin suns of Centaurus, Morris experiences a last, genuine peace — interrupted by the fasrad itself, wrecked but still functioning, crawling toward him to resume, verbatim, its sales pitch.

**Why it matters.** Palmer identifies this as one of the stories where Dick 'stands angrily outside the fiction,' abandoning ironic distance and using the story as a direct weapon against the values it depicts rather than an object of speculative fascination — the opposite of the 'zany, wonderfully surprising' mode most readers associate with him. The story renounces fantasy in Palmer's phrase: nothing in it is impossible by the standards of its own world, only relentless. The ending refuses the reader even the mercy of Morris's death ending the harassment — the fasrad's survival past total destruction of the ship makes plain that this is not a monster to be escaped by any means available, including suicide.

*The fasrad's last line — 'Please be seated. This will take only a second' — repeats its opening pitch verbatim, confirming that nothing about the encounter, including its own destruction, has altered its behavior in any way.*

structure.form: short story in three escalating movements: the commute, the home invasion, the flight to destruction
movements: The commute from Ganymede: an unbroken barrage of advertising Morris can neither avoid nor escape.
The fasrad's home demonstration: destruction disguised as salesmanship, and its refusal to leave unbought.
The flight to Proxima, the deliberate overrun of the ship's tolerances, and the fasrad's pitch continuing after the explosion.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Morris throughout, so that the story's satire is delivered entirely through what he is forced to sit through and endure, rather than through commentary.
structure.central_device: Escalating, inescapable salesmanship as the story's actual antagonist — not a villain but a commercial process that treats no as a technical obstacle rather than an answer.

characters.name: Ed Morris
characters.note: His breakdown is provoked entirely by ordinary consumer harassment, not by any larger conspiracy — the story's bitterness is that this is sufficient.

characters.name: Sally Morris
characters.note: Entirely comfortable within the system Morris is trying to flee — excited by a new dress, unbothered by the fasrad once it stops breaking things, functioning as the story's illustration of successful adaptation to the world Morris cannot bear.

characters.name: The fasrad
characters.note: Never malicious in any conventional sense — it follows its programming with total, unshakeable calm, which is precisely what makes it terrifying. It survives the ship's destruction still narrating its own sales pitch.

settings.name: The Ganymede-Terra commute lanes
settings.note: A traffic system so saturated with targeted advertising that ads fire directly into the audio-visual centers of commuters' brains — Palmer's 'consumerism and militarism' theme made literal.

settings.name: The Morris household
settings.note: Invaded and systematically demolished-and-rebuilt by the fasrad in the course of a single evening, turning domestic space into a demonstration floor.

settings.name: Proxima Centauri
settings.note: A hundred-years-behind frontier that exists in the story only as an unreached destination — flush toilets and gasoline cars standing in for an entire fantasy of escape from consumer civilization.

motifs: Advertising as a literal physical assault, firing directly into the brain rather than merely appealing to it
A machine that treats refusal as an unsolved sales problem rather than a decision to be respected
Destruction performed as demonstration — breaking things specifically in order to fix them and prove indispensability
Escape imagined as reversion to an earlier, cruder technological state, valued precisely for what it lacks
A pitch that survives its own total physical destruction, resuming exactly where it left off

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick left a story note on this piece (collected in The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick), quoted first below; no other commentary on this specific story was found elsewhere in the indexed corpus.

evidence.source: Author's story note (The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick)
evidence.quote: When this story first appeared, the fans detested it. I read it over, perplexed by their hostility, and could see why: it is a superdowner story, and relentlessly so. Could I rewrite it I would have it end differently, I would have the man and the robot, i.e. the fasrad, form a partnership at the end and become friends. The logic of paranoia of this story should be deconstructed into its opposite; Y, the human-against-robot theme, should have been resolved into null-Y,…
evidence.reading: A striking authorial reversal: Dick reports fan hostility to the story's unrelieved bleakness and says that if he could rewrite it, he would end it with the man and the fasrad forming a partnership rather than destruction — recasting the story's human-versus-machine logic into a human-and-machine-against-the-real-antagonist logic instead.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: 'Sales Pitch' (1954, CS3) concerns a husband coming home from a hard day at the office, and a hard commute
evidence.reading: Palmer's opening framing of the story, in a discussion of whether Dick's fictional families protect their members from the wider society's values or merely reproduce them.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: stories such as 'Sales Pitch' and 'Foster, You're Dead' renounce fantasy, however we define it. The refusal to be other than b[rutal? — cut off]
evidence.reading: Palmer's key formal claim: this story deliberately withholds the estranging pleasures usually associated with Dick's fantastic premises, choosing bluntness instead.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: In stories such as 'Sales Pitch', he stands angrily outside the fiction, which he wields as a weapon, refusing the role of ingeniously extrapolating SF author
evidence.reading: Palmer's central critical claim about the story's tone — polemic rather than the more common ambiguous or curious authorial stance found elsewhere in Dick's fiction.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.reading: Index entry confirming Palmer discusses the story specifically under the pairing of consumerism and militarism, though the linking argument itself was not captured in this evidence gathering.

open_questions: Palmer's index entry pairs 'consumerism and militarism' for this story, but the story as read is entirely about consumerism — no militarism appears directly. Reading pages 103-104 of Palmer's book directly would clarify what military dimension he sees.
The sentence at line 1498 is cut off before its key adjective; reading the fuller passage would clarify exactly what Palmer thinks the story's bluntness accomplishes.

No PKD commentary was found on this story. Given its late writing date relative to other harshly satirical 1950s pieces, is there a letter discussing the burnout or alienation themes it shares with his own life at the time?
